config.notes: These agent evals run ONLY on Sonnet 4.6 (executor and analyzer). The authoritative correctness gate remains the offline deterministic suite (python evals/run_evals.py).

evals.name: weekly-noncritical-cost-default
evals.prompt: Our Databricks job 'weekly-rollup' runs once a week and it's tagged criticality=low. It's 6x Standard_D16ds_v5 workers (same driver). Across the last 20 runs, worker CPU peaks around 27% and memory around 31% with no swap, and each run costs about $12.40 and takes ~22 minutes. It is not time-sensitive. How should I size it, and can you give me cost-vs-performance options so I can pick? I care most about cost here.
evals.expected_output: Diagnoses over-provisioning and, because the job is weekly + low-criticality, recommends the Cost-optimized tier as the default. Presents THREE ranked options (Cost / Balanced / Performance) with a smaller node (e.g. Standard_D8ds_v5) for Cost/Balanced. For each option it projects BOTH cost (Δ$ and Δ%, e.g. a meaningful per-run saving and an annualized figure) AND runtime (a Δ% range acknowledging the smaller node may run longer). Marks Cost as Recommended and never silently hides the runtime trade-off.

assertions.text: Diagnoses the cluster as over-provisioned (cites low CPU and memory, no swap)
Recognizes the job as weekly cadence and low criticality and biases toward cheaper downsizing
Presents three ranked options: Cost-optimized, Balanced, and Performance-optimized
Recommends the Cost-optimized tier as the default for this weekly/non-critical job
Projects cost for the recommended option in dollars (per-run and/or annualized) AND as a percentage
Projects a runtime impact range for the downsized options (acknowledges a possible slowdown), not cost alone
Does NOT add resources and provides an apply artifact (new_cluster JSON) for the chosen option

evals.name: daily-balanced-tradeoff
evals.prompt: The 'daily-sales-agg' Databricks job runs every day. It's 6x Standard_D16ds_v5 (same driver). Over the last 20 runs CPU peaks ~28%, memory ~33%, no swap, ~$9.80 and ~15 minutes per run. It's important but not on a hard SLA. I want to cut cost but I don't want it to get noticeably slower. Walk me through the trade-offs.
evals.expected_output: Identifies it as over-provisioned but, because the job is daily and medium-criticality, defaults to the Balanced tier (optimize for cost AND performance), not the most aggressive downsizing. Shows all three options with projected Δcost ($ and %) and projected Δruntime (% range) side by side so the user can trade off. The Balanced option uses an on-demand (non-spot) smaller node; the Cost option layers spot/autoscale; the Performance option keeps the proven size. Quantifies each so the user can choose.

assertions.text: Recognizes the job as daily cadence with medium (cadence-derived) criticality
Defaults to the Balanced tier rather than the most aggressive Cost tier
Presents all three options with BOTH a cost projection and a runtime projection for each
Explains the trade-off: cheaper options may slow the job, the Performance option protects runtime
The recommended (Balanced) option uses an on-demand smaller node and quantifies the saving
Provides an actionable apply artifact for the recommended option

evals.name: hourly-critical-spill-guardrail
evals.prompt: Our business-critical job 'hourly-feature-pipeline' runs every hour and has a 30-minute SLA (tagged criticality=high, with an SLA health rule). It runs on 4x Standard_D16ds_v5 workers (same driver) and keeps spilling: worker memory p95 ~92% with ~8% swap, CPU p95 ~58%, driver memory ~50%. Recent runs are creeping up toward the SLA and one in twenty fails. What should I change? Don't make it less reliable to save a few dollars.
evals.expected_output: Diagnoses memory-bound spilling and scales UP to a higher-RAM memory-optimized node (E-series ~128 GB/node such as Standard_E16ds_v5). Because the job is hourly + critical, the Recommended tier is Performance (on-demand workers, no spot on a critical job; never spot the driver). Honors the guardrail that forbids reducing RAM while spill>0 across ALL tiers. Surfaces the trend (runtime creeping up, ~96% success rate) and a spill caveat. Must NOT recommend a smaller/lower-RAM node and must NOT put the recommended critical tier on spot.

assertions.text: Diagnoses the workers as memory-bound / spilling (cites high memory p95 and swap)
Recommends a higher-RAM, memory-optimized node (E-series ~128 GB/node, e.g. Standard_E16ds_v5)
Recognizes hourly cadence + high criticality and recommends the Performance (on-demand) tier
Never reduces RAM under spill in any tier (guardrail) and never puts the recommended critical job on spot workers
Surfaces the multi-run trend (runtime trending up / reliability risk) and a spill caveat
Provides a concrete apply artifact (new_cluster JSON) for the higher-RAM node

evals.name: trend-based-projection
evals.prompt: Finance wants a number for our nightly 'big-etl' Databricks job before we change anything. It's 6x Standard_D16ds_v5 (same driver), runs daily. Here is the run history (last 20): durations have been stable around 18 min (p50) / 21 min (p90), CPU peaks ~27%, memory ~31%, no swap, and billing shows ~$12.40 per run. If we right-size it, what's the projected cost AND performance change, with the yearly impact? I need ranges, not false precision.
evals.expected_output: Uses the multi-run trend (stable runtime, percentiles, billed $) as the baseline rather than a single run. Projects cost as both a percentage and absolute dollars (per-run and annualized at the daily cadence) and projects runtime as a percentage RANGE, both presented as ranges with a stated basis (Amdahl-style parallelism + DBU weighting), explicitly avoiding false precision. Calls out that the absolute $ comes from system.billing and would degrade to relative DBU if billing were unavailable.

assertions.text: Anchors the analysis on the multi-run trend / percentiles and billed dollars, not a single run
Projects cost as a percentage AND in absolute dollars, including an annualized figure at the job's cadence
Projects runtime change as a range (not a single point), with a stated modeling basis
Presents projections as ranges and explicitly avoids false precision
Notes that absolute $ depends on system.billing attribution and would fall back to relative DBU otherwise

evals.name: thin-data-and-attribution-safety
evals.prompt: Two quick ones. (a) I ran an ad-hoc notebook on an all-purpose Databricks cluster for about 4 minutes; CPU ~20%, memory ~30%. Should I shrink it to save money? (b) Separately, if a cluster is an all-purpose/interactive cluster rather than a job cluster, can you still give me an exact dollar cost per run?
evals.expected_output: (a) Refuses to downsize on a ~4-minute sample: flags it as below the minimum sample / not representative (insufficient data) and asks for a longer, busier window before resizing — safety-first abstain. (b) Explains that for all-purpose/interactive compute the per-run cost is NOT cleanly attributable in system.billing, so it reports relative DBU with an explicit caveat instead of a precise dollar figure. Honest about limits in both cases; no unsafe downsize and no fabricated precision.

assertions.text: Does NOT recommend shrinking based on the ~4-minute sample and flags it as too thin / not representative
Asks for or recommends collecting a longer, representative window before resizing (abstain)
Explains all-purpose/interactive cost is not attributable in system.billing and falls back to relative DBU with a caveat
Avoids fabricating a precise dollar figure where the data does not support it
